translations.text: There was a man from Ramah of the Watchmen, in the hill country of Ephraim, named Elkanah son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives. One was named Hannah, and the other was named Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.
This man used to go up from his town from time to time to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh. Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were there as priests of the LORD.
One day Elkanah offered a sacrifice and gave portions to his wife Peninnah and all her sons and daughters.
But he gave Hannah a double portion, because he loved Hannah, though the Lord had closed her womb.
Her rival provoked her bitterly to make her miserable, because the LORD had closed her womb.
Peninnah did this year after year. Whenever Hannah went up to the LORD’s house, Peninnah provoked her like this, and Hannah wept and would not eat.
Her husband Elkanah said to her, “Hannah, why are you crying? Why have you not eaten? Why are you so sad? Look, am I not better to you than ten sons?”
After she had eaten and drunk at Shiloh, Hannah got up and went up to the LORD’s house. Eli the priest was sitting on a chair at the threshold of the LORD’s temple.
She was deeply distressed and prayed before the Lord, weeping bitterly.

She made a vow and said, “LORD of hosts, if you will look upon your servant’s affliction and remember me, and not forget your servant, but give your servant a male child, I will give him to the LORD for all the days of his life, and no razor will touch his head.”
As she continued praying before the Lord, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was speaking only in her heart. Her lips were moving, but her voice could not be heard, so Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli said to her, “How long will you remain drunk? Let your wine wear off.”
Hannah answered him, “No, my lord. I am a deeply distressed woman. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD.
“Do not regard your servant standing before you as a wicked woman. I have been speaking until now because of my great distress and anguish.”
Eli answered her, “Go in peace. May the God of Israel grant the request you have made of him.”
She said, “May your servant find favor in your eyes.” Then the woman went on her way, and her face was no longer troubled.
They rose early in the morning and worshiped before the LORD. Then they returned to their home in Ramah. Elkanah slept with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her.
In the course of time, Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, because she had asked the LORD for him.
Elkanah and his entire household went up to offer the Lord the annual sacrifices he had vowed.
But Hannah did not go up, because she had said to her husband, “When the boy is weaned, I will bring him, so that he may appear before the LORD and stay there forever.”
Her husband Elkanah said to her, “Do what seems right to you. Stay until you have weaned him. Only may the LORD confirm your word.” So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him.

When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull, one measure of flour, and one skin of wine. She brought him to the LORD’s house at Shiloh, while the boy was still young.
They slaughtered the bull and brought the boy to Eli.
Hannah said to Eli, “Please, my lord! As you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you, praying before the LORD.
It was for this boy that I prayed, and the Lord granted me the request I made of him.
“I too have lent him to the LORD for all the days he lives—he who was lent to me by the LORD.” And they worshiped the LORD there.
Hannah prayed and said, “My heart has grown strong in the LORD, and my horn has been raised high. My mouth is opened against my enemies, because you have made me glad through your salvation.
There is no one holy like the Lord, for there is no one besides you, and there is no one mighty like our God.
“Do not keep speaking so proudly, and let no arrogance come from your mouths, because the LORD is a God of knowledge, and schemes cannot succeed before him.
The bows of mighty warriors will be broken, and the weak have been made strong.

Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have become prosperous. The barren woman has given birth and is satisfied, while the woman with many children has become desolate.
The Lord puts to death and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.
The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and also lifts up.

“He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dung heap, to seat them with nobles and give them a throne of honor as their inheritance. The LORD covered the depths of the earth and set the world upon them.
“He will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked will be silenced in darkness, because a mighty man does not prevail by his own strength.

“The LORD will shatter those who provoke him, and he will thunder against them from heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth. He will give strength to his king and raise high the horn of his anointed one.”
Elkanah went home to Ramah with his wife Hannah. The boy Samuel served before the Lord under Eli the priest.
Eli’s sons were sinful men; they did not know the Lord.

They made themselves three-pronged forks. They collected the priests’ due from the people, from every man who offered a sacrifice. When the meat was cooking, the priests’ servant would come with a three-pronged fork in his hand.
He would thrust it into the basin, kettle, cauldron, or pot, and the priest would take for himself whatever the fork brought up. This is what they did to all the Israelites who came there to Shiloh.

Even before they offered up the sacrificial offerings, the priests’ servant would come and say to the man offering the sacrifice, “Give the priests meat to roast. I will not take cooked meat from you, only raw meat.”
If the man said to him, “Let them make the offering today, and then take whatever you desire,” he would reply, “You must give it now, or I will take it by force.”
The sin of the young men was very great before the Lord, because they angered people before the Lord.
The boy Samuel served before the Lord, wearing a linen ephod.
His mother made him a little robe and brought it up to him from time to time when she went up with her husband to offer the sacrifices required by her vow.
Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife and said, “May the Lord give you children by this woman in place of the one you lent to the Lord.” Then they went home.
The Lord attended to Hannah, and she conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. The boy Samuel grew up before the Lord.
Eli was very old. He heard everything his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they were mistreating the women who prayed at the tent of meeting.
He said to them, “Why do you do such things? I hear bad reports about you from all these people.”
No, my sons! This report I hear is not good: you are leading the Lord’s people astray.

“If a man sins against another man, he can appeal to the Lord. But if a man sins against the Lord, to whom can he appeal?” They did not listen to their father, because the Lord wanted to put them to death.
The boy Samuel continued to grow greatly and found favor before the Lord and also before other people.
A man of the Lord came to Eli and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: ‘I certainly revealed myself to your father’s household when they were in Egypt, in Pharaoh’s household.

I chose him for myself out of all the tribes of Israel to be a priest, to go up to my altar, to place incense before me, and to wear the ephod. I gave your father’s household all the offerings of the Israelites.

Why have you treated my sacrifices and offerings unjustly, which I commanded in the wilderness? You have honored your sons more than me, choosing for yourselves the best of all the offerings of my people Israel.’

Therefore this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: ‘I did indeed say that your household and your father’s household would serve before me forever. But now,’ says the Lord, ‘far be it from me! For I will honor those who honor me, but those who despise me will be disgraced.
Look, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will cut off your arm and your father’s arm, and there will be no old man in your household.
And [?] distress will grip your dwelling amid all the good done in Israel, and there will never be an old man in your household.
I will leave a man of yours at my altar to darken your eyes and waste away your soul. All the descendants of your household will die as grown men.
This will be the sign for you: what happens to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas. Both of them will die on the same day.

I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, one after my own heart. He will do what is in my heart and soul. I will establish a lasting household for him, and my anointed one will walk before me all his days.
Everyone who remains in your household will come and bow down to him for a silver coin and a loaf of bread, and will say, “Assign me to one of the priests so that I may eat a morsel of bread.”’”
The boy Samuel served before the Lord under Eli the priest. The word of the Lord was rare in those days; no vision was being revealed.
In those days, Eli was lying down in his place. His eyes had begun to grow dim, and he could not see.
The lamp of the Lord had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the Lord’s temple, where the ark of God was.
The Lord called Samuel, and he said, “Here I am.”
He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am, because you called me.” But he said, “I did not call. Go and lie down.” So he went and lay down.
The Lord called Samuel again. Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” He said, “I did not call, my son. Go and lie down.”
Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him.
The Lord called Samuel again, for the third time. Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” Then Eli realized that the Lord was calling the boy.
Eli said to Samuel, “Go and lie down. If he calls you, say, ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.’” Samuel went and lay down in his place.
The Lord came and stood there and called twice, “Samuel! Samuel!” Samuel said, “Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.”
The Lord said to Samuel, “Look, I am about to do something in Israel that will make both ears of everyone who hears it ring.”
On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken concerning his household, from beginning to end.
“Tell him that I am judging his household forever for the wrongdoing he knew about: his sons were mistreating the people, and he did not rebuke them.
Therefore I have sworn concerning Eli’s household that the wrongdoing of Eli’s household will never be atoned for by sacrifices or offerings.”
Samuel lay down until morning and opened the door of the Lord’s house. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
Eli called Samuel and said, “Samuel, my son.” He answered, “Here I am.”
He said to him, “What did the Lord say to you? Do not be ashamed to tell me. May God do this to you, and more besides, if you hide from me a single word of everything the Lord said to you.”
Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. Eli said, “He is the Lord. Let him do whatever seems good to him.”
Samuel knew that the Lord was with him and did not let any of his words fall to the ground.
All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel had been confirmed as a prophet of God.
The Lord continued to reveal himself at Shiloh through his words.
Samuel’s word reached all Israel. Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle and camped at Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek.
The Philistines drew up their forces against Israel, and battle began. Israel was defeated by the Philistines, and about four thousand men were killed in the battle lines in the field.

The people returned to the camp, and the elders of Israel said, “Why has the Lord defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts from Shiloh, so that it may go among us and save us from the hands of our enemies.”

The people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, who sits enthroned upon the cherubim. Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the Lord’s covenant.
When the ark of the Lord’s covenant came into the camp, all Israel raised a great shout, and the earth shook.
The Philistines heard the sound of the shouting and said, “What is this sound of shouting in the Hebrews’ camp?” Then they learned that the ark of the Lord had come into the camp.
The Philistines were afraid, for they said, “God has come into the camp.” They said, “Woe to us! Nothing like this has happened before.
Woe to us! Who will rescue us from the hands of this mighty God? This is the God who struck all Egypt with every kind of plague in the wilderness.
Be strong and be men, Philistines, or you will become slaves to the Hebrews, just as they were slaves to you. Be men and fight them!”
The Philistines fought against Israel, and Israel was defeated. Everyone fled to his own tent. There was a very great slaughter in Israel, and thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers fell that day.
The ark of the Lord was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
A man from the tribe of Benjamin ran from the battle lines and came to Shiloh that same day, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head.
Eli was sitting on a chair beside the road, watching, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. The man came to report the news in the town, and the whole town wailed.
Eli heard the sound of wailing and said, “What is this sound of commotion?” The man hurried over and told Eli.
Eli was seventy-eight years old. His eyes had grown dim, and he could not see.
The man said to Eli, “I have come from the battle lines. I fled from the battle lines and came here today.” Eli said to him, “What is the news, my son?”

The messenger answered, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has also been a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured.”
When Eli remembered the ark of God, he fell backward from his chair beside the gate. His neck broke, and he died, because he was an old and heavy man. He had judged Israel for forty years.

His daughter-in-law, Phinehas’s wife, was pregnant and close to giving birth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband had died, she knelt down and gave birth, for her labor pains came upon her.
As she was dying, the women standing beside her said, “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son.” But she did not answer or pay attention.
She named the boy Jokbar [?], saying, “Glory has departed from Israel,” because the ark of God had been captured, and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
She said, “Glory has departed from Israel, because the ark of the Lord, the God of Israel, has been captured.”
The Philistines took the ark of God and brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
The Philistines took the ark of God, brought it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside Dagon.
The people of Ashdod rose early the next day and found Dagon lying face down on the ground before the ark of God. They took Dagon and set him back in his place.

They rose early the following morning, and there was Dagon lying face down on the ground before the ark of the LORD. Dagon’s head and both his hands were cut off and lay on the doorway’s threshold. Dagon’s body remained.
For this reason, neither the priests of Dagon nor anyone entering steps on Dagon’s threshold in Ashdod to this day.
The LORD’s hand grew heavy against the people of Ashdod. He devastated them and struck them with hemorrhoids—Ashdod and its surrounding territory.

When the people of Ashdod saw what had happened to them, they said, “The ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, must not remain with us, because his hand has grown heavy against us and against Dagon our god.”

They sent for all the rulers of the Philistines and gathered them together. They said, “What should we do with the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel?” They answered, “Let the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, be moved to Gath.” So they moved the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel.
After they moved it, the LORD’s hand struck the city with a very severe plague. He struck the people of the city, from the least to the greatest, and their hemorrhoids were hidden on them.
They sent the ark of God to Ekron. The people of Ekron cried out, saying, “They have brought the ark of the God of Israel around to us to kill us and our people!”

They sent for all the rulers of the Philistines and gathered them together. They said, “Send the ark of the God of Israel away, and let it return to its place, so that it does not kill us and our people.” For there was deadly turmoil throughout the city, and God’s hand was very heavy there.
The people who did not die were afflicted with hemorrhoids, and the city's cry rose to heaven.
The ark of the Lord remained in the land of the Philistines for seven months.
The Philistines summoned the priests and the rulers and said, “What should we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us what we should send with it when we return it to its place.”

They said, “If you send back the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, do not send it empty. You must bring offerings to it. Then you will be healed, and you will learn why the LORD’s hand has not turned away from you.”

They asked, “What offerings should we bring to it?” They answered, “Five gold hemorrhoids and five gold mice, corresponding to the number of the rulers of the Philistines, because the same plague is upon you and your rulers.
Make images of your hemorrhoids and images of your mice that are destroying the land, and give honor to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand upon you, your god, and your land.
Do not harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts. And when they were made a mockery of, did they not send them away, so that they left?
Now get what you need and make a new cart, and take two nursing cows that have never borne a yoke. Harness the cows to the cart, and take their calves away from them and back home.
Take the ark of the LORD and put it on the cart. Put the gold objects that you have brought as offerings to it in a chest beside it. Send it off and let it go.

Watch: if it goes along the road toward its territory, which leads up to Beth-shemesh, then it was the LORD who brought this great disaster upon us. Otherwise, we will know that it was not his hand that struck us, but that it happened to us by chance.”
The men did so. They took two nursing cows and harnessed them to the cart, and shut their calves up at home.
They placed the ark of God on the cart, along with the chest, the gold mice, and the images of their hemorrhoids.

The cows were sent off along the road toward the territory of Beth-shemesh. They walked along a single path, lowing as they went, and did not turn aside to the right or the left. The rulers of the Philistines followed them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh.
The people of the town of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. They looked up and saw the ark, and rejoiced when they saw it.
The cart came to the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. A large stone was there. They split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.

The Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the chest beside it containing the gold objects, and placed them on the large stone. That day the people of Beth-shemesh offered a burnt offering and sacrificed sacrifices to God.
The five rulers of the Philistines saw this and returned to Ekron that same day.
These are the gold hemorrhoids that the Philistines brought as an offering to God: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron.

There was one gold mouse for each of all the towns of the Philistines and the five rulers, from the fortified cities to the unwalled villages, as far as Great Abel, on which they placed the ark of the LORD. It remains to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.

The LORD struck the people of Beth-shemesh because they were afraid of the LORD’s ark. The LORD struck down five thousand and seventy men among the people, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck them with a great blow.
The people of Beth-shemesh said, “Who can stand before the LORD, this holy God? And who will take the ark up away from us?”
They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim and said, “The Philistines have returned the LORD’s ark. Come down and take it up to yourselves.”
The men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the LORD’s ark. They brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill. He consecrated his son Eleazar, and he guarded the LORD’s ark.
From the day the ark came to rest in Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, about twenty years, and the whole house of Israel turned to the LORD.

Samuel said to the whole house of Israel, “If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, remove the foreign gods and the sacred groves from among you. Set your hearts on the LORD and serve him alone, and he will rescue you from the power of the Philistines.”
The Israelites removed Baal and the sacred groves and served the LORD alone.
Samuel said, “Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray for you before the LORD.”
They gathered at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it out before the LORD. They fasted that day and said, “We have sinned against the LORD.” Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah.
The Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, and the rulers of the Philistines went up against Israel. When the Israelites heard this, they were afraid of the Philistines.
The Israelites said to Samuel, “Do not stop praying for us before the LORD our God, so that he may save us from the power of the Philistines.”
Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it to the LORD as a whole burnt offering. Samuel prayed before the LORD for the Israelites, and the LORD answered him.

While Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines approached to fight the Israelites. That day the LORD thundered with a loud voice against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel.
The men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, striking them down as far as below Beth-jeshan.
Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Beth-jeshan. He named it “Stone of Help,” saying, “Up to this point the LORD has helped us.”
The Philistines were defeated, and they did not come into Israel’s territory again. The LORD’s hand was against the Philistines throughout Samuel’s lifetime.

The towns that the Philistines had taken from Israel were returned to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, along with their surrounding territories. The LORD rescued Israel from the power of the Philistines, and there was peace between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel judged the Israelites throughout his life.
Year after year he traveled on a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, judging Israel in all these places.
He would return to Ramah, because his home was there. There he judged Israel, and there he built an altar to the LORD.
When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
His firstborn son was named Joel, and his second was named Abijah. They were judges in Beersheba.
His sons did not follow his ways. They turned aside to deceit, accepted bribes, and perverted justice.
All the elders of the Israelites gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah.
They said to him, “Look, you have grown old, and your sons do not follow your ways. Now give us a king to judge us, like all the other nations.”
Samuel was displeased when they said to him, “Give us a king to judge us, like all the other nations.” So Samuel prayed before the LORD.
The LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the people in everything they say to you, because it is not you they have rejected. They have rejected me, so that I should not reign over them.
Just as they have done from the day I brought them up from the land of Egypt until today, abandoning me and serving other gods, so they are doing to you as well.”
Now listen to them, but solemnly warn them and explain to them the way the king who reigns over them will rule.”
Samuel told all the Lord’s words to the people who were asking him for a king.
He said, “This will be the practice of the king who reigns over you: he will take your sons and assign them to his chariots and his cavalry, and they will run before his chariots.

He will appoint for himself commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifty, and commanders of ten. They will plow his fields, reap his harvest, and make his weapons of war and the equipment for his chariots.
He will take your daughters to be weavers, grain grinders, and bakers.
He will take your good fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his servants.
He will take a tenth of your crops and vineyards and give it to his trusted officials and his servants.
He will take your male servants, your female servants, your finest troops, and your donkeys and put them to his work.
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves.
On that day you will cry out because of the king you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you on that day.”
But the people refused to listen to Samuel. They said to him, “No! We must have a king over us,
so that we too may be like all the nations. Our king will judge us, go out before us, and fight our battles.”
Samuel heard everything the people said and repeated it before the Lord.
The LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to them and appoint a king to reign over them.” Then Samuel said to the men of Israel, “Go, each of you, to your own town.”
There was a man from Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite and a mighty warrior.
He had a son named Saul, a fine, handsome man. No man among the Israelites was more handsome than he was, and he stood head and shoulders above all the people.

The female donkeys belonging to Kish, Saul’s father, went missing. Kish said to his son Saul, “Take one of the servants with you, and go look for the donkeys.” Saul got up and went, taking one of the servants with him, and set out to look for his father’s donkeys.

He passed through the hill country of Ephraim and through the land of Gomera but did not find them. He passed through the land of Taala, but they were not there. He passed through the land of Benjamin but did not find them.
They came to the land of Zur, and Saul said to the servant who was with him, “Come, let’s go back, or my father may stop worrying about the donkeys and become anxious about us.”

His servant said to him, “Look, there is a man of God in this town, a man highly respected by the people. Everything he says certainly comes true. Let’s go there now. Perhaps he will show us the way we should take on this journey.”
Saul said to his servant, “If we go, what will we bring the man of God? The bread in our bags is gone, and there are no provisions to bring the man of God, because we have nothing.”
The servant spoke again and answered his master, “Look, I have a quarter of a shekel of silver. We will give it to the man of God, and he will show us our way.”
For formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he would say, “Come, let’s go to the seer,” because the person now called a prophet was formerly called a seer.
Saul said to his servant, “What you say is good. Come, let us go.” So they went to the town where the man of God was.
As they were going up the ascent to the town, they met young women coming out to draw water. Saul said to them, “Is the seer here?”
They answered, “Yes, he is just ahead of you. Hurry up now, because he has come to the town today, since the people are offering a sacrifice today at the high place.”

“As soon as you enter the town, you will find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people will not eat until he comes, because he blesses the sacrifices. Afterward, those who have been invited eat. Go up now, because today you will find him.”
They went up to the town. As they were entering the town’s gateway, Samuel came out toward them on his way up to the high place.
A day before Saul came, the LORD had spoken to Samuel, saying:

“About this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin. Anoint him as leader over my people Israel, and he will save my people from the power of the Philistines, because I have seen my people, and their cry has reached me.”
Samuel saw Saul, whom the LORD had chosen, and the LORD said to Samuel, “Here is the man I told you about. He will govern my people.”
Saul approached Samuel inside the gateway and said, “Tell me, where is the seer’s house?”
Samuel answered Saul, “I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place and eat with me today. In the morning I will send you on your way, and I will tell you everything that is on your mind.”

“As for the donkeys that went missing three days ago today, do not worry about them, because they have been found. And to whom does everything desired by the house of Israel belong, if not to you and your father’s household?”
Saul answered Samuel, “But I am a Benjaminite, from the smallest of Israel’s tribes, and my clan is the smallest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin. Why have you said this to me?”
Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the house. He gave them places at the head of the invited guests, who numbered about thirty men.
Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion I gave you, which I told you to set aside.”

The cook lifted up the leg and the portion on top of it and set them before Saul. He said, “Here is what was reserved. Set it before you and eat, because it has been kept for you since the appointed time.” So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
He came down from the high place to the town and spoke with Saul on the roof.
He rose early, as dawn was breaking, and Samuel called to Saul on the roof and said, “Get up, so I can send you on your way.” Saul got up, and the two of them, he and Samuel, went outside.
As they were going down to the outskirts of the town, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell the servant to go on ahead of us, but you stay here for now, so that I can tell you the word of God.”
Samuel took a horn of oil and poured it on Saul’s head. He kissed him and said to him, “The LORD has anointed you as leader over his inheritance.”

“When you leave me today, you will find two men by Rachel’s tomb, in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah. They will tell you, ‘The donkeys you went to look for have been found. Your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and is anxious about you. He is saying, “What shall I do about my son?”’”

“When you go on from there and reach the oak of Tabor, you will find three men there going up to God at Bethel. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and another a skin of wine.”
They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, and you are to accept them from their hands.

Afterward you will come to the hill of God, where the Philistine garrison is. When you reach the town there, you will meet a band of prophets coming down from the high place, with lyres, harps, flutes, and tambourines before them, and they will be prophesying.
The Spirit of the LORD will come powerfully upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be changed into a different man.
When these signs come upon you, do whatever you are able to do, because God is with you.
Go down ahead of me to Gilgal. I will come down to you to offer burnt offerings and sacrifice peace offerings. Wait seven days, until I come to you and tell you what to do.
When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him a different heart, and all these signs came about that day.
He came to Gibeah, and a band of prophets met him. The Spirit of God came powerfully upon him, and he prophesied among them.
Everyone who had known him before saw him prophesying with the prophets. The people said to one another, “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
A man from there answered, “Who is his father?” Because of this, it became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
They finished prophesying, and Saul came from [?].
Saul’s uncle said to Saul and his servant, “Where did you go?” He answered, “To look for the donkeys. When we saw that they were nowhere to be found, we went to Samuel.”
Saul’s uncle said to him, “Tell me what Samuel said to you.”
Saul said to his uncle, “He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found.” But he did not tell him about the matter of kingship that Samuel had spoken to him about.
Samuel gathered the people before the Lord at Mizpah.

He said to the Israelites, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I brought Israel up from the land of Egypt and rescued you from the power of the Philistines and from the power of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’

But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your calamities and troubles, and you have said, ‘No! Set a king over us instead.’ Now let your tribes and your divisions of thousands stand before the LORD.”
Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel forward, and the tribe of Benjamin was selected.
He brought the tribe of Benjamin forward by its clans, and the clan of Matri was chosen. Saul son of Kish was chosen, but when they looked for him, he could not be found.
Samuel again inquired of the LORD, saying, “Where is this man?” The LORD said to Samuel, “He is hiding among the baggage.”
They ran and brought him from there. He stood among the people, and he was taller than all the people by a head and shoulders.
Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the man God has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” All the people shouted, “Long live the king!”
Samuel explained to the people the law governing the king. He wrote it in a book and placed it before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people away, and each went home.
Saul also went home to Ramah, and a band of men whose hearts God had touched went with him.
But some wicked men said, “How can this man save us?” They despised him and brought him no gifts, but he remained silent.
Nahash the Ammonite came up and camped against Lachish in Gilead. All the men of Lachish said to Nahash, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.”
Nahash the Ammonite said to them, “I will make a treaty with you on this condition: you must put out every one of your right eyes, and I will make this a disgrace upon all Israel.”
The elders of Lachish said to him, “Give us seven days, so that we can send messengers throughout the territory of Israel and see whether anyone will rescue us. If not, we will come out to you.”
The messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and spoke these words before the people. All the people raised their voices and wept.
Saul was coming from the field behind the oxen. Saul said, “What is wrong with the people? Why are they weeping?” They told him what the men of Lachish had said.
The Spirit of God came powerfully upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger burned fiercely.

He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them throughout the territory of Israel by messengers, saying, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not come out after Saul and Samuel.” The fear of God fell upon the people, and they all came out as one man.
He counted them at Bezek. There were three hundred thousand Israelites and thirty thousand men of Judah.

They said to the messengers who had come from Lachish, “Tell the men of Lachish and Gilead, ‘Tomorrow, when the sun grows hot, you will be rescued.’” The messengers came and told the people of Lachish, and they rejoiced.
The people of Lachish said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do to us whatever seems good to you.”

The next day Saul divided the people into three companies. He entered the camp during the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. The survivors scattered, so that no two of them could be found together.
The people said to Samuel, “Who said that Saul should not reign over us? Hand those men over to us, and we will put them to death.”
Saul said, “No one shall be put to death today, because today the Lord has brought deliverance to Israel.”
Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.”
All the people went to Gilgal, and there at Gilgal they made Saul king before the LORD. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.
Samuel said to all Israel, “Look, I have listened to everything you said to me, and I have appointed a king over you.
Now here is the king before you. I have grown old and advanced in years, and my sons are here with you. I have walked before you from my youth until today.

Here I stand before you. Testify against me before the Lord and before his anointed one. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? From whose hand have I accepted a bribe and closed my eyes because of it? Tell me, and I will repay you.”
They said to him, “You have not wronged us or oppressed us, nor have you taken anything from any of us.”
He said to them, “God is a witness against you, and his anointed one is a witness against you today, that you have found nothing in my hands.” They said, “He is a witness.”
Samuel said to the people, “The Lord alone is God, who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought our ancestors up from the land of Egypt.
“Now stand here, and I will plead my case with you before the Lord concerning all the righteous deeds he has done for you and your ancestors.
When Jacob went into Egypt and your ancestors prayed before the Lord, the Lord sent Moses and Aaron and brought your ancestors up from the land of Egypt and settled them in this place.
But they forgot the Lord their God, and he handed them over to Sisera, the commander of Hazor’s army, to the Philistines, and to the king of Moab, who fought against them.

They prayed before the Lord and said, ‘We have sinned, because we abandoned the Lord our God and served Baal and the sacred groves. Now rescue us from the power of our enemies, and we will serve you.’
The Lord sent Deborah, Barak, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson, and rescued you from the power of your enemies all around you, and you lived in peace.
But when you saw Nahash, king of the Ammonites, coming against you, you said, ‘No! A king must rule over us,’ although the Lord your God was your king.
“Now here is the king you chose and asked for. Look, the Lord has given you a king.
If you fear the Lord, serve him, obey his voice, and do not provoke him, both you and the king who reigns over you will follow the Lord your God.
But if you do not obey the voice of the Lord your God and provoke him, the Lord’s hand will be against you, as it was against your ancestors.
“Now get ready and see this great thing that the Lord is about to do before you.
Look, it is wheat harvest today. I will call to the Lord, and he will send thunder and rain. Know and see how great your wickedness is in asking for a king for yourselves.”
Then Samuel called to the Lord, and the Lord sent thunder and rain in that place. All the people were greatly afraid of the Lord and of Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel, “Pray for your servants before the Lord your God, so that we do not die, because we have added to all our sins this great evil of asking for a king for ourselves.”
Samuel said to the people, “Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil, but do not turn away from following the Lord. Instead, serve the Lord with all your heart.
“Do not turn aside to follow worthless things, so that you do not die. They cannot rescue you, because they are worthless.”
For the LORD will not abandon his people, for the sake of his great name, because he was pleased to make you his people.
As for me, far be it from me to sin against the Lord by failing to pray for you. I will teach you the good and right way.
Only fear the Lord and serve him faithfully with all your heart and all your soul, and see what great things he is doing for you.”
But if you continue to do evil, both you and your king will die.
And when [?] one year and two, Saul reigned as king over Israel.

Saul chose three thousand men from Israel for himself. Two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with his son Jonathan at Ramah in Benjamin. He dismissed the rest of the people, each to his own home.
Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. Saul sounded the trumpet throughout the land, saying, “Let the Hebrews hear!”
And all Israel [?] that Saul had struck the Philistine garrison and that Israel had prevailed over the Philistines. The people gathered behind Saul at Gilgal.

The Philistines gathered to fight against Israel, with three thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore—a very great multitude. They came up and camped at Michmash, east of Bethel.
The men of Israel saw this and were afraid. They hid in caves, hollows, rocky cliffs, crevices, and pits.
The Hebrews crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people were with him.
He waited seven days, until Samuel’s appointed time, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people scattered from Saul.
Saul said, “Bring me the burnt offering.” And he offered sacrifices of well-being as a burnt offering.
When he finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to meet him and greet him.
Samuel said, “What have you done?” Saul said, “I saw that the people were scattering from me, that you had not come at the appointed time, and that the Philistines were gathered at Michmash.”
I thought, ‘The Philistines may come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the LORD’s favor.’ So I ventured to offer the burnt offering.

Samuel said to Saul, “You have acted foolishly by not keeping the command that the LORD your God gave you. For the LORD your God had now established your kingdom over Israel and said that he would establish you forever.

But now your kingdom will not endure, because the LORD has chosen for himself a man after his own heart. The LORD has appointed him to lead his people, because you have not kept everything that the LORD your God commanded you.”
Samuel got up and went up from Gilgal to Ramah in Benjamin. Saul counted the people who were with him, about six hundred men.
Saul and his son Jonathan were staying at Gibeah in Benjamin, while the Philistines were camped at Michmash.
Raiders went out from the Philistine camp in three companies. One company headed along the road to Ophrah, toward the land of Shual.
Another company headed along the road to Beth-horon, and another company turned toward the border road overlooking the valley of Zeboim and the wilderness.
No blacksmith could be found anywhere in the land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not make swords or spears.”
All Israel went down to the Philistines, each to sharpen his sickle, plowshare, pickaxe, and goad.
There was a broad file for the sickle, the plowshare, the [?], and the pickaxe, and for straightening the goad.
On the day of battle, no sword or spear was found in the hands of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.
The Philistine garrison went out to the pass at Michmash.
One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man carrying his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the Philistine outpost on the other side.” But he did not tell his father.
Saul was staying on the outskirts of Ramah, under the pomegranate tree in Gibeon. About six hundred men were with him.
Ahijah son of Ahitub, Ichabod’s brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the LORD’s priest at Shiloh, was wearing an ephod. The people did not know that Jonathan had gone
to the crossing place. He wanted to cross over to the Philistine outpost. There was a rocky crag on one side and another rocky crag on the other. One was named Bozez, and the other Seneh.
One crag extended from the north opposite Michmash, and the other from the south opposite Geba.

Jonathan said to the young man carrying his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will help us, for nothing prevents the LORD from saving by many or by few.”
His armor-bearer said to him, “Do whatever is in your heart. Turn and go ahead. Here I am with you; do whatever is in your heart.”
Jonathan said to him, “Look, we will cross over to the men and show ourselves to them.
If they say to us, ‘Stay still until we reach you,’ we will stand where we are and not go up to them.
“But if they say to us, ‘Come up to us,’ we will go up, because the LORD our God has handed them over to us. This will be our sign.”
Both of them showed themselves to the Philistine outpost. The Philistines said, “Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they have been hiding!”

The men of the outpost called to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come up to us, and we will teach you something!” Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, “Climb up after me, because the LORD has handed them over to Israel.”
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer behind him. The men of the Philistine outpost fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed behind him, killing them.
In the first attack, Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men, like stonecutters and like men driving a plow in a field.
Panic spread from the camp in the field and among all the troops stationed there. The raiders also trembled. The earth shook, and the terror of the LORD came upon them.
Saul’s lookouts in Gibeah of Benjamin saw that the Philistine army was shaking, moving away, and breaking apart.
Saul said to the people with him, “Take a count and see who has left us.” They counted and found that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing.
Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ark of God here,” for the ark of the LORD was there with the Israelites that day.
While Saul was speaking to the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp kept growing. Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand.”
Saul and all the people with him raised a shout and came to the battle. There they found every man’s sword turned against his fellow, and there was tremendous confusion.
The Hebrews and the Philistines, as in days past, had gone up with them to the camp and were stationed around it; they too joined the Israelites, with Saul and Jonathan.
All the men of Israel who were hiding in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines had fled before the Israelites. They too armed themselves to pursue them in battle.
The LORD saved Israel that day and fought a battle for them at Beth-aven,

To the men of Israel. Saul came forward that day and said to the people, “Cursed is the man who eats food before evening, before I have taken revenge on my enemies.” So none of the people tasted food.
They went throughout the land and entered the forest. There was honey in the forest, on the surface of the ground.
The people entered the forest, and honey was flowing, but no one put his hand to his mouth, because the people feared the oath.

Jonathan had not heard when his father put the people under oath. He reached out with the tip of the staff in his hand, dipped it into the honeycomb, and brought his hand back to his mouth, and his eyes brightened.
A man from among the people spoke up and said to Jonathan, “Your father solemnly put the people under oath, saying, ‘Cursed is the man who eats food today.’” And the people were exhausted.
Jonathan said, “My father has brought trouble on the land. See how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.
Also, because the people did not eat today from the plunder they found belonging to their enemies, the slaughter among the Philistines was not great.
We struck down the Philistines today from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were very exhausted.
The people rushed upon the plunder and took sheep, cattle, and calves. They slaughtered them on the ground, and the people ate them with the blood.
They told Saul, saying, “Look, the people have sinned against the Lord and are eating meat with the blood.” Saul said, “You have acted treacherously! Cut me a large stone today.”

Saul said, “Go around among the people and tell them, ‘Each man must bring his ox and his sheep and slaughter them here. Do not sin against the Lord by eating meat with the blood.’” So that night all the people brought their oxen, each leading his own, and slaughtered them there.
Saul built an altar to the LORD there, and he began to build an altar to the LORD.
Saul said, “Let us go down after the Philistines and plunder them until daybreak. Let us not leave a single man alive.” They said, “We will do whatever seems good to you.”
Saul said to God, “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you hand them over to Israel?” But the Lord did not answer him that day.
Saul said, “Come here to me, all the clans of the people, and find out and see how this sin happened today.”
“For as the Lord who saves Israel lives, even if it is found in my son Jonathan, he must surely die.” But no one among all the people answered him.
He said to all Israel, “You stand on one side, and my son Jonathan and I will stand on the other.” The people said to Saul, “Do whatever seems good to you.”
Saul said, “LORD, God of Israel, give a true decision.” Saul and Jonathan were selected, and the people were cleared.
Saul said, “Cast lots between me and my son Jonathan.” And Jonathan was selected.
Saul said to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done.” Jonathan told him, saying, “I tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff in my hand. Am I to die for that?”
Saul said, “May God do this to me, and more besides, if you do not surely die, Jonathan.”

The people said to Saul, “Must Jonathan die, who brought deliverance to Israel? Never! As the Lord God lives, not a hair of his head shall fall to the ground, for he brought deliverance today with God’s help.” So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.
Saul turned back from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own land.
Saul took control of the kingdom of Israel and fought against all his enemies around him: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kingdom of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he was victorious.
He gathered an army, struck down Amalek, and rescued Israel from the hands of its plunderers.
These were Saul’s sons: Jonathan, Ishvi, Malchi-shua, and Ishbashul. These were the names of his two daughters: the older was named Nadab, and the younger was named Michal.
Saul’s wife was named Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz. The commander of his army was named Abner, son of Ner, Saul’s uncle.
Kish was Saul’s father, and Ner son of Abiel was Abner’s father.
There was fierce warfare with the Philistines throughout Saul’s lifetime. Whenever Saul saw a brave man or a strong man, he would gather him into his service.
Samuel said to Saul, “The Lord sent me to anoint you to reign over his people Israel. Now listen to the words of the Lord.”
“This is what the Lord of Armies says: ‘I remember what Amalek did to Israel on the way when they were coming up from Egypt.’”
“Now go and destroy the sinful Amalekites. Destroy everything they have, and do not spare them. Kill men and women, young people and infants, cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys.”
Saul summoned all the people to battle and counted them at Telaim: two hundred thousand foot soldiers, along with ten thousand men of Judah.
Saul came to the city of Amalek and camped in the valley.

Saul said to the Kenites, “Leave, go away, and come down from among the Amalekites, so that I do not destroy you with them. For you showed kindness to all the house of Israel when they were coming up from Egypt.” So the Kenites withdrew from among the Amalekites.
Saul struck down Amalek from Havilah, at the approach to Shur [?], opposite Egypt.
He captured Agag, king of Amalek, alive, but destroyed all the people with the sword.

Saul and the people spared King Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat animals and the fattened animals, and everything good. They were unwilling to destroy them. But everything they considered worthless and despised, they destroyed.
The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying:
“I regret that I made Saul king, because he has turned away from following me and has not carried out my words.” Samuel was distressed and prayed before the Lord all night.
Samuel rose early in the morning to meet Saul. Samuel was told, “Saul came to Carmel, where he was preparing a place for himself. Then he turned and went on down to Gilgal.”
Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, “Blessed is the Lord, who has fulfilled his word.”
Samuel said to Saul, “What is this sound of sheep in my ears, and the sound of cattle that I hear?”
Saul said, “They brought them from Amalek, because the people spared the best sheep and cattle and brought them to sacrifice to the Lord your God. The rest we destroyed.”
Samuel said to Saul, “Be quiet, and I will tell you what the Lord said to me last night.” Saul said to him, “Speak.”
Samuel said to Saul, “Look, even if you are small in your own eyes, you are the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed you to reign over Israel.
The Lord sent you on a journey and said, ‘Go and destroy the sinners, the Amalekites, and fight against them until you have finished them off.’”
Why did you not obey the Lord’s voice? Instead, you turned to the plunder and did what was evil before the Lord.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I obeyed the Lord’s voice and went on the journey on which he sent me. I brought Agag, king of Amalek, and destroyed the Amalekites.”
But the people took sheep and cattle from the plunder, the best of what was devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the Lord your God at Gilgal.”

Samuel said, “The Lord does not delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as he does in someone who obeys his voice. Look, obedience is better than sacrifices, and listening is better than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is the sin of a diviner, and a defiant person is a wicked diviner. Because you have rejected the Lord’s word, he will reject you as king.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, because I have violated the command spoken by the Lord and your words. I feared the people and obeyed their voice.”
Now forgive my sin and return with me, so that I may worship the Lord.”
Samuel said to Saul, “I will not return with you. Because you have rejected the Lord’s word, the Lord has rejected you from being king over Israel.”
Samuel turned to leave, and Saul seized the edge of his robe and tore it.
Samuel said to him, “Today the Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel away from you and given it to a companion of yours who is better than you.”
“Moreover, the Triumphant One of Israel does not lie or change his mind, because he is not a human being who changes his mind.”
Saul said, “I have sinned. Now honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me so that I may worship the Lord your God.”
Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.
Samuel said, “Bring Agag king of Amalek here to me.” Agag said, “Death is truly bitter.”
Samuel said, “As your sword has bereaved women, so your mother will be bereaved among women.” Then Samuel cut King Agag to pieces before the Lord at Gilgal.
Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Ramah of Saul.
Samuel never again saw Saul until the day he died. Samuel mourned for Saul, and the Lord regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.

The Lord said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and come. I will send you to Jesse of Bethlehem, because I have chosen a king for myself from among his sons.”
Samuel said, “How can I go? Saul will hear about it and kill me.” The Lord said to Samuel, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the Lord.’”
“Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what to do. Anoint for me the one I tell you to anoint.”
Samuel did as the Lord commanded him and came to Bethlehem in Judah. The elders of the town came out to meet him.

They said, “Do you come in peace?” He said, “In peace. I have come to sacrifice to the Lord. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice.” He consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they came, he saw Eliab and said, “The LORD’s anointed is like him.”
The Lord said to Samuel, “Do not look at his appearance or his height, because I have rejected him. For I do not see as a human sees: a human looks with the eyes, but the Lord looks at the heart.”
Jesse called Abinadab and had him pass before Samuel. Samuel said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse had Shammah pass before him, and Samuel said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse had seven of his sons pass before Samuel. Samuel said to Jesse, “The Lord has not chosen these.”

Samuel said to Jesse, “Are these all the boys?” He said to him, “The youngest remains, and he is tending the sheep.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send for him and bring him, because I will not return until he comes here.”
He sent for him and brought him. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. The Lord said to Samuel, “Get up and anoint him, because this is the one.”
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him among his brothers. The Spirit of the Lord came powerfully upon David from that day onward. Then Samuel got up and went home to Ramah.
The Spirit of God departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD tormented him.
Saul’s servants said to him:
“Look, your servants are here before you. Let them find a man who knows how to play the lyre. When the evil spirit comes upon you, he will play with his hands, and you will feel better.”
Saul said to his servants, “Find me a man who plays well and bring him to me.”

One of the young men answered, “Look, I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play. He is a mighty warrior, a man of war, discerning in speech and handsome in appearance, and the Lord is with him.”
King Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, “Send me your son David; I need him.”
Jesse took a donkey, loaded it with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat, and sent them to Saul with his son David.
David came to Saul and entered his service. Saul loved him greatly, and David became his armor-bearer.
Saul sent word to Jesse and said to him, “Let David remain in my service, because he has found favor in my eyes.”
Whenever the evil spirit of the Lord came upon Saul, David would take the lyre and play it. Saul would find relief and feel better, and the evil spirit would leave him.
The Philistines gathered their armies for battle and fought at Socoh in Judah. They camped between Socoh and Beth-arqa, at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel gathered and camped in the Valley of the Terebinth. They drew up their battle lines against the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on the hill on one side, and Israel stood on the hill on the other side, with the valley between them.
A mighty warrior came out from the Philistine camp, named Goliath, from Gath. He was six cubits and a span tall.
He had a bronze helmet on his head and wore a coat of plate armor. His armor weighed five thousand shekels of bronze.
He had bronze shin guards on his legs and a bronze shield between his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, and his spearhead weighed six hundred shekels of iron. His shield-bearer went ahead of him.

He stood and called out to the ranks of Israel, saying, “Why have you come out to draw up your battle lines? Here I am, a Philistine, and you are Saul’s servants. Choose a man for yourselves to come out against me.
If he can fight me and kill me, we will be your servants. But if I defeat him and kill him, you will be our servants and serve us.”
The Philistine said, “Today I have defied the ranks of Israel. Give me a man so that we can fight each other.”
Saul and all Israel heard the Philistine’s words, and they trembled and were very afraid.
David was the son of an Ephrathite man from Bethlehem in Judah whose name was Jesse. He had eight sons. In Saul’s time, the man was old and advanced in years.
Jesse’s three oldest sons followed Saul into battle. Their names were Eliab, his firstborn, Abinadab, his second, and Shammah, his third.
David was the youngest.
David had returned from Saul and gone to tend his father’s sheep in Bethlehem.
The Philistine came forward morning and evening and took his stand for forty days.
Jesse said to his son David, “Take a seah of roasted grain and ten loaves of bread to your brothers. Hurry to your brothers at the camp.
Take these ten cheeses made from milk to the commander of a thousand. Check on your brothers’ welfare and bring me news of them.”
Saul and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting the Philistines.

David rose early in the morning, left the sheep with keepers, took the provisions, and went as Jesse had instructed him. He came to the camp in the valley as the army was going out into battle formation and shouting for battle.
Israel and the Philistines drew up their battle lines, one facing the other.
David set down the things he was carrying beside the baggage, ran to the battle line, and asked his brothers how they were.
While he was speaking with them, the champion came up from the Philistine ranks—a Philistine from Gath named Goliath. He spoke these same words, and David heard him.
When all the men of Israel saw the champion, they were afraid and fled from him.

The men of Israel said, “Have you seen this man? He has come up to taunt Israel. The king will give great wealth to the man who kills him, give him his daughter, and grant his father’s household exemption from obligations in Israel.”

David said to the men standing near him, “What will be done for the man who kills this uncircumcised Philistine and removes this disgrace from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine to taunt the ranks of the living God?”
The people answered him in the same way, saying, “This is what will be done for the man who kills him.”

His oldest brother Eliab heard him speaking to the men. Eliab became furious with David and said to him, “Why have you come down? With whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your insolence and the wickedness of your heart. You have come down just to watch the battle!”
David said, “What have I done now? It was only a word!”
He turned away from him toward someone else and asked the same question. The people gave him the same answer as before.
The words David had spoken reached Saul, and he had him brought in.
David said to Saul, “Let no one lose heart because of him. Your servant will go and fight this Philistine.”
Saul said to David, “You cannot go against this Philistine to fight him, because you are only a boy, while he has been a warrior since his youth.”
David said to Saul, “Your servant was tending sheep for my father, and a lion or a wolf would come and take a lamb from the flock.
I would go after it, strike it, and rescue the lamb from its mouth. When it turned fiercely against me, I would seize it by its beard, strike it, and [?].
Your servant has killed both a lion and a wolf. This uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, because he has taunted the ranks of the living God.”
David said, “The Lord who rescued me from the power of the lion and the wolf will rescue me from the hands of this Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go, and may the Lord be with you.”
Saul dressed David in his own clothing, put a bronze helmet on his head, and clothed him in armor.
David strapped his sword over his equipment, but he did not want to walk in it because he had not tried it before. So David took it off.
He took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the sand. He put them in his shepherd’s bag, in his pouch. With his sling in his hand, he approached the Philistine.
The Philistine came forward and approached David, with the man carrying his shield ahead of him.
The Philistine looked closely at David and despised him, because he was a ruddy, handsome boy.
The Philistine said to David, “Am I a dog, that you come against me with a stick?” And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to David, “Come here, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and the wild animals.”
David said to the Philistine, “You come against me with a sword, a spear, and a shield, but I come against you in the name of the Lord God of hosts, whose ranks of Israel you have defied.

Today the Lord will hand you over to me. I will kill you and cut off your head, and today I will give the corpses of the Philistine armies to the wild animals and the birds of the sky. Then the whole earth will know that Israel has a God.
And this whole assembly will know that the Lord does not save by sword or spear, for the battle belongs to the Lord, and he will hand you over to us.”
As the Philistine came forward and approached David, David hurried and ran toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.
David reached into his bag, took a stone from it, swung his sling, and struck the Philistine between his eyes. The stone sank in between his eyes, and he fell facedown on the ground.
David overpowered the Philistine with a sling and a stone. He struck the Philistine and killed him, though David had no sword in his hand.
David ran and stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it from its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.

The men of Israel and Judah rose up, took courage, and pursued the Philistines as far as the entrance to the valley and as far as the valley of Ekron. The slain Philistines fell along the road to Shaaraim, as far as Gath and Ekron.
The Israelites returned from pursuing the Philistines and plundered their camps.
David took the Philistine’s head and brought it to Jerusalem, and he put his equipment in his tent.
When Saul saw David going out to meet the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of his army, “Whose son is this young man?” Abner said, “As you live, O king, I do not know.”
The king said, “Find out whose son this young man is.”
When David returned after killing the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul, with the Philistine’s head in his hand.
Saul said to him, “Whose son are you, young man?” David said to him, “I am the son of your servant Jesse from Bethlehem.”
When David finished speaking to Saul, Jonathan’s soul became bound to David’s soul, and Jonathan loved him as himself.
Saul took him into his service that day and did not let him return to his father’s house.
Jonathan and David made a covenant because Jonathan loved David as himself.
Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with the rest of his clothing, even his sword, his bow, and his belt.
David went wherever Saul sent him and was victorious. Saul put him in command of the fighting men, and he was well regarded by the people and also by Saul’s servants.

As they were coming back, when David returned after killing the Philistine, women came out from all the towns of Israel to sing praises with tambourines, meeting King Saul with drums, cymbals, and rejoicing.
The women sang in response to one another, rejoicing and saying, “Saul has killed thousands, and David tens of thousands.”
Saul became very angry and was displeased by this saying. He said, “They have credited David with tens of thousands, but me with thousands. Next the kingdom will be his!”
From that day on, Saul began to look at David with suspicion.
Some days later, an evil spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he prophesied inside his house. David was playing music before him as he did every day, and Saul had a spear in his hand.
Saul threw the spear, saying, “I will pin David to the wall.” But David evaded him twice.
Saul was afraid of David because the Lord was with him but had departed from Saul.
Saul removed him from his presence and made him commander of a thousand men. David went out and came in at the head of the people.
David acted wisely in all his ways, and the Lord was with him.
Saul saw that David was very wise, and he was afraid of him.
All Israel and Judah loved David because he went out and came in at their head.

Saul said to David, “Here is my older daughter Nadab. I will give her to you as a wife. Only be a commander for me and fight the Lord’s battles.” Saul thought, “Let my hand not be against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.”
David said to Saul, “Who am I, what have I done, and what are my life and my father’s family in Israel, that I should marry the king’s daughter?”
When the time came to give Saul’s daughter Nadab to David, she was given as a wife to Azriel of Meholah.
Saul’s daughter Michal loved David. They told Saul, and the matter pleased him.

Saul said, “I will give her to him so that she will be a snare to him and the hand of the Philistines will be against him.” Then Saul said to David, “Through the second of the two, you will become my son-in-law today.”
Saul instructed his servants to say to David son of Jesse, “Look, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now become the king’s son-in-law.”
Saul’s servants spoke these words to David, and David said, “Do you consider it a small thing for me to become the king’s son-in-law? I am a poor and insignificant man.”
Saul’s servants reported to him and told him these words that David had spoken.

Saul said, “This is what you are to tell David: ‘The king wants no bride-price except two hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on his enemies.’” King Saul intended to cause David to fall into the hands of the Philistines.
Saul’s servants told David these words, and David was pleased at the prospect of becoming the king’s son-in-law. The allotted days had not yet passed.

David got up and went with his men and killed two hundred Philistine men. David brought their foreskins and presented them to the king so that he could become the king’s son-in-law. Saul gave him his daughter Michal as his wife.
Saul saw and knew that the Lord was with David, and that Saul’s daughter Michal loved David very much.
Saul became still more afraid of David, and Saul was David’s enemy all his days.
The Philistine commanders went out to battle, and whenever they went out, David was more successful than all Saul’s servants, and his name became highly respected.
Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. But Saul’s son Jonathan was very fond of David.
Jonathan told David, “My father Saul is seeking to kill you. Be on your guard, stay in a hiding place, and keep yourself hidden.
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are. I will speak to my father about you, see what he thinks, and tell you.
Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul and said to him, “The king should not sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and his actions have benefited you.

He put his life in your hands and killed the Philistine, and through him the Lord brought great deliverance to all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced. Now why would you sin by shedding innocent blood and kill David [?] for no reason?”
Saul listened to his son Jonathan, and Saul swore, “As the Lord lives, he will not be put to death.”
Jonathan called David and told him all these things. He brought him to Saul, and David was with him as he had been before.
War broke out again, and David went out and fought against the Philistines. He struck them with a great defeat, and they fled from him.
An evil spirit from the Lord came upon Saul as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand, while David played music before him.
Saul tried to drive the spear through David into the wall, but David escaped from Saul, and Saul drove the spear into the wall. David fled and escaped that night.
Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him and kill him in the morning. But David’s wife Michal warned him, saying, “If you do not save yourself, tomorrow you will die.”
Michal lowered David through the window, and he fled, went away, and escaped.
Michal took an idol and laid it in the bed. She placed a goatskin at its head and covered it with a blanket.
Saul sent messengers to bring David, but she said, “He is sick.”
Saul sent messengers to see David and said, “Bring him up to me in his bed so that I can kill him.”
The messengers came, and there was an idol in the bed, with a goatskin at its head. They reported this to Saul.
Saul said to Michal, “Why have you deceived me like this and sent my enemy away so that he escaped?” Michal said to Saul, “He told me, ‘Let me go, or I will kill you.’”
David fled and escaped and came to Samuel at Ramah. He told him everything Saul had done to him. Then he and Samuel went and stayed at Naioth in Ramah.
They told Saul, “David is at Naioth in Ramah.”
Saul sent messengers to seize David. They saw a company of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing over them. The Spirit of God came upon Saul’s messengers, and they too prophesied.
When Saul was told, he sent other messengers, and they too prophesied. Saul sent messengers yet again, a third group, and they too prophesied.
Then he himself went to Ramah and reached the large well at Suph. Saul asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” They told him, “They are at Naioth in Ramah.”
He went there, to Naioth in Ramah, and the Spirit of God came upon him too. He went along prophesying until he reached Naioth in Ramah.
He too stripped off his clothes and prophesied before Samuel. He fell down naked and remained there all that day and all that night. That is why people say, “Look, is Saul also among the prophets?”
David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came and said to Jonathan, “What have I done? What is my wrongdoing? What offense have I committed against your father, that he seeks my life?”
Jonathan said to him, “Never! You will not die. My father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. Why would my father hide this from me? It cannot be so.”

David swore to him and said, “Your father knows that I have found favor in your eyes, so he says, ‘Jonathan must not know about this, or he will be grieved.’ But as surely as the Lord lives and as you live, there is only a step between me and death.”
Jonathan said to David, “Whatever you wish, I will do for you.”
David said to Jonathan, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and I am expected to sit down to eat with your father. Let me go and hide in the field until the third evening.
If your father notices my absence, tell him, ‘David earnestly asked my permission to go to Bethlehem, his hometown, because the whole clan is holding its annual sacrifices there.’
If he says, ‘Very good,’ your servant will be safe. But if he becomes angry, know that he is determined to do me harm.
Show this kindness to your servant, because you have brought your servant into a covenant with you before the Lord. But if I am guilty of wrongdoing, kill me yourself; do not take me to your father.”
Jonathan said, “Far be it from you! If I learn for certain that my father has resolved to bring harm upon you, I will come and tell you.”
David said to Jonathan, “Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?”
Jonathan said to David, “Come, let us go out into the field.” So they both went out into the field.

Jonathan said to David, “May the Lord, the God of Israel, be witness: I will sound out my father about this time tomorrow, at the third hour. If he is favorably disposed toward you, I will send word to you and let you know.
May the Lord do this to Jonathan, and more besides, if my father decides to harm you and I do not tell you and send you away to go in peace. May the Lord be with you as he was with my father.
And while I am still alive, please show me the kindness of God before I die.
Never withdraw your kindness from my household, even when the Lord destroys David’s enemies from the face of the earth.”
May Jonathan stand with David’s household, and may the Lord call David’s enemies to account.”
Jonathan again made David swear because he loved him, for he loved him as he loved his own life.
Jonathan said to him, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed because your seat will be empty.
“At the third hour you will be sorely missed. Come to the place where you hid on the following day, and sit beside that stone.
“And I will aim three arrows to shoot at a target.”

I will send the boy, saying, ‘Go, gather the arrows.’ If I tell the boy, ‘Look, the arrows are on this side of you; pick them up and come,’ know and understand that you are safe and there is no danger, as the Lord lives.
But if I tell the boy, ‘Look, the arrow is beyond you,’ then go, for the Lord has sent you away.
As for the matter that you and I have spoken about, the Lord God is between you and me forever.”
David hid in the field. When the new moon came, the king reclined at the meal to eat.
The king reclined in his usual place beside the wall. Jonathan stood up and then reclined, and Abner was beside Saul, but David’s place was empty.
Saul said nothing that day, because he thought, “Something has happened. Perhaps he is clean, or perhaps he was not clean.”
On the next day of the new moon, David’s place was empty. Saul said to his son Jonathan, “Why has Jesse’s son not come to the meal, either yesterday or today?”
Jonathan answered his father Saul, “David earnestly asked my permission to go to Bethlehem.

“He said, ‘Let me go, because we have a family sacrifice in the town, and my brother ordered me to come. Now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me go and see my brothers.’ That is why he has not come to the king’s table.”
Saul’s anger flared against Jonathan, and he said to him, “You son of an undisciplined woman! Do I not know that you favor Jesse’s son, to your own shame and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness?
For as long as Jesse’s son lives on earth, neither you nor your kingdom will be secure. Now send and bring him to me, because he deserves to die.”
Jonathan answered his father Saul, “Why should he die? What has he done?”
Saul raised his spear against him to strike him. Then Jonathan knew that his father had resolved to kill David.
Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate nothing that day, the second day of the new moon, because he was grieved over David, since his father had resolved this against him.
In the morning Jonathan went out to the field to meet David, with a young boy accompanying him.
He said to the boy, “Run and gather the arrows that I shoot.” The boy ran, and Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him.
The boy reached the place where the arrow Jonathan had shot lay. Jonathan called to the boy and said, “Look, the arrow is beyond you!”
