Jonathan called after the boy, “Hurry! Be quick! Do not stop!” Jonathan’s boy gathered the arrows and brought them to his master.
The boy knew nothing about it; only Jonathan and David knew the matter.
Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, “Go, take them into the town.”

The boy went inside, and David rose from beside the stone and came to Jonathan. He fell facedown to the ground and bowed three times. They kissed each other and wept over each other, but David wept more.
Jonathan said to David, “Go in peace. We have both sworn in the Lord’s name, saying, ‘May the Lord stand between me and you, and between my descendants and your descendants forever.’”
Jonathan rose and went into the town.
David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech was startled when he met David and said to him, “Why have you come alone, with no one accompanying you?”

David said to Ahimelech the priest, “The king has entrusted me with a task and told me, ‘Let no one know anything about the mission on which I am sending you or the instructions I have given you.’ I have directed the young men to a secluded, hidden place.
Now, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever can be found.”
The priest answered David, “I have no ordinary bread on hand, but there is holy bread, provided the young men have abstained from sexual intercourse.”

David answered the priest, “Sexual intercourse has been permitted to us since yesterday and the day before, when I set out. The young men’s vessels are holy, though the journey is an ordinary one, and today it will also be sanctified through the vessels.”

The priest gave him the holy bread, because there was no bread there except the bread of the Presence, which is removed from before the Lord so that fresh, warm bread can be put in its place on the day it is taken away.
Now one of Saul’s servants was there that day, detained before the Lord. His name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul’s shepherds.
David said to Ahimelech, “Do you have a sword or spear here on hand? I did not bring either my sword or my spear with me, because the king’s business was urgent.”

The priest said, “The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want to take it, take it, because there is no other here.” David said, “There is none like it. Give it to me.”
David got up and fled from Saul that day, and he came to Achish king of Gath.

The servants of Achish said to him, “This is the king of the land of Israel! This is the man whom the daughters of Israel used to praise, saying, ‘Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.’”
David took these words to heart and became very afraid of Achish king of Gath.
He changed his behavior before him and acted drunk in their sight. He sat on the threshold of the gate and let his saliva run down his beard.
Achish said to his servants, “Look, you can see that the man is mad. Why have you brought him to me?
Am I out of my mind, that you have brought this man to act like a madman before me? Is this man to enter my house?”
David went away from there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. His brothers and his father’s entire household heard about it and went down to him there.
Everyone who was in distress, everyone who had a creditor, and everyone who was bitter in spirit gathered around him. He became their leader, and there were about four hundred men with him.
David went from there to Mizpah in Moab. He said to the king of Moab, “Let my father and mother stay with you until I know what God will do for me.”
He left them with the king of Moab, and they stayed with him all the time that David was in Mizpah.
The prophet Gad said to David, “Do not stay in Mizpah. Go into the land of Judah.” So David went and entered the forest of Hereth.

Saul heard that David and the men with him had been discovered. Saul was sitting in Gibeah under the almond tree on the height, with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing around him.
Saul said to his servants standing around him, “Listen, Benjaminites! Will the son of Jesse give all of you fields and vineyards? Will he make all of you commanders of thousands and hundreds?

For all of you have rebelled against me, and no one tells me about my son’s covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you feels sorry for me or tells me that my son has stirred up my servant against me to lie in ambush, as he is doing today.”
Doeg the Edomite, who was in charge of Saul’s servants, answered, “I saw David come to Nob, to Ahimelech son of Ahitub the priest.”
He inquired of God for him and gave him equipment and provisions. He also gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
The king sent for Ahimelech son of Ahitub the priest and his father’s entire household, the priests in Nob. They all came to the king.
Saul said, “Listen now, son of Ahitub.” He answered, “Here I am, my lord.”

Saul said to him, “Why have you and the son of Jesse conspired against me? You gave him bread and a sword and consulted God for him, so that he could rise against me and lie in ambush, as he is doing today.”
Ahimelech the priest answered the king, “Who among all your servants is like David—faithful, the king’s son-in-law, obedient to your commands, and honored in your household?

Was today the first time I consulted God for him? Far be it from me! Let the king not charge his servant or my father’s entire household with this matter, for your servant knew nothing at all about this whole affair, great or small.”
The king said, “You will certainly die, Ahimelech—you and your father’s entire household.”

The king said to the guards standing around him, “Turn and kill the priests of God, because they have sided with David. They knew he was fleeing but did not tell me.” But the king’s servants would not raise their hands to strike down the priests of God.
The king said to Doeg, “You turn and attack the priests.” Doeg attacked the priests and killed eighty-five men that day who wore linen ephods.
He gave him the town of the priests, and he killed its people with the sword, men and women, young people and infants, and also the cattle, donkeys, and sheep with the sword.
One son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to join David.
Abiathar told David that Saul had killed God’s priests.
David said to Abiathar, “I knew that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would certainly tell Saul. I am responsible for every life in your father’s household.”
Stay with me and do not be afraid, for whoever seeks my life also seeks yours, and a protector is with me.”
They told David, “Look, the Philistines are attacking Keilah and plundering the threshing floors.”
David consulted the Lord, saying, “Shall I go and attack these Philistines?” The Lord said to him, “Go, attack the Philistines and save Keilah.”
David’s men said to him, “[?] We are afraid here. How can we go to Keilah against the Philistine battle line?”
David consulted God again, and the Lord answered him, “Get up and go down to Keilah, for I am handing the Philistines over to you.”
David and his men went to Keilah and fought the Philistines. They drove off their livestock, and he inflicted a great defeat on them. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech fled to David at Keilah, he brought an ephod down with him.
Saul was told that David had entered Keilah. Saul said, “God has handed him over to me, for he has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars.”
Saul summoned all the people for battle, to go down to Keilah and besiege David and the men with him.
David learned that Saul was plotting harm against him, and he said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring me the ephod.”
David said, “Lord, God of Israel, your servant has heard for certain that Saul intends to come to Keilah to destroy the town because of me.”
“Will the leaders of the town hand me and the men with me over to Saul?” The Lord said, “They will hand you over. Get up and leave the town.”
David and the men with him, about six hundred men, got up and left Keilah. They returned and told Saul that David had escaped from Keilah, and he gave up going out.
David stayed in the wilderness strongholds and lived in the hill country in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul searched for him every day, but God did not hand him over to him.
David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph, in the thicket.
Jonathan son of Saul got up and went to David in the woods and strengthened his hands in God.

He said to him, “Do not be afraid, because my father Saul will not be able to get his hands on you. You will reign over Israel, and I will be with you, and you will live. My father Saul also knows that this is so.”
The two of them made a covenant before the LORD, who sits enthroned upon the cherubim, in the valley, and Jonathan went home.
The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah and said to him, “Look, David is hiding among us in the strongholds, in the woods, in the hills, in the valley south of Jeshimon.”
Now come down to us, just as you desire, and we will hand him over to the king.”
Saul said to them, “May God bless you, because you have had compassion on me.
“Go back and investigate where he is staying. Find out and see the place where he goes and who has seen him there, because I have been told that he is very crafty.

Find out and inspect all the hiding places where he hides, and return to me to give me definite information. Then I will go with you. If he is in the land, I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah.”
They got up and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah beside Jeshimon.
Saul and his servants went to search for David. David was told, and he went down to the rock and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. Saul heard and pursued David into the wilderness of Maon.

Saul went along one side of the mountain, and David and his men along the other side. David was hurrying to escape from Saul, while Saul and his servants were surrounding David and his men to capture them.
A messenger came to Saul and said to him, “Come quickly, because the Philistines have encamped throughout the land!”
Saul turned back from pursuing David and went to meet the Philistines. That is why they called that place “the [?] of Division.”
David went up from there and stayed in the strongholds in the hills.
When Saul returned from pursuing the Philistines, they informed him, saying, “Look, David is in the strongholds in the hills.”
Saul took three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went to search for David and his men along the slopes of the mountain of the wild goats.
He came to the sheepfold beside the road, where there was a cave. Saul entered the cave and slept there, while David and his men were staying in the depths of the cave.

David’s men said to him, “This is the day when the Lord said to you, ‘Look, I am handing your enemy over to you. Do to him whatever seems good to you.’” David got up and quietly cut off a corner of Saul’s cloak.
Afterward David’s conscience troubled him because he had cut off a corner of Saul’s cloak.
David said to the men with him, “May the Lord forbid that I should do this to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, and lay my hand on him, because he is the Lord’s anointed.”
David rebuked the men with him with these words and did not allow them to attack Saul. Saul got up, left the cave, and went on his way.
Afterward David got up, came out of the cave, and called after Saul, “My lord the king!” Saul turned around, and David fell facedown on the ground and bowed.
David said to Saul, “Do not listen to people who say, ‘Look, David is seeking to harm you.’

“Look, see with your own eyes today that the Lord handed you over to me today in the cave. The men with me said to kill you, but I spared you. I said, ‘I will not lay my hand on my lord, because he is the Lord’s anointed.’

Turn and look at the corner of your cloak in my hand. When I cut off the corner of your cloak, I did not kill you. Know and see that I have done no evil or wrongdoing, and I have not sinned against you. Yet you are hunting me to take my life.
May the LORD judge between me and you, and may the LORD avenge me against you. But my hand will not be against you.
As the ancient proverb says, ‘Wickedness comes from the wicked.’ But my hand will not be against you.
Whom have you come out after, king of Israel? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A single flea?”
“May the Lord be judge and judge between you and me. May he see, judge my case, and rescue me from your hands.”
When David finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said to him, “Is that your voice, my son David?” Saul raised his voice and wept.
Saul said to David, “You are more righteous than I am, because you have repaid me with good, while I have repaid you with evil.
Today you have shown that you have treated me well: the Lord handed me over to you, but you did not kill me.
“When a man finds his enemy and sends him safely on his way, may the Lord repay him with good. May the Lord repay you with good on my behalf today for what you have done for me.”
Now I know that you will certainly become king, and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands.
Swear to me by the Lord that you will not destroy my descendants after me or wipe out my name from my father’s family.”
David swore to Saul, and Saul went home. David and the men with him went up to Mizpah.
Samuel died, and all Israel gathered and mourned for him. They buried him in his tomb at Ramah. David got up and went down to the wilderness of Paran.
There was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel. The man was very wealthy and had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. And when he was shearing his sheep at Carmel
The man's name was Nabal, and his wife's name was Abigail. The woman was beautiful in appearance and [?], but the man Nabal was harsh, evil in his dealings, and doglike.
David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
David sent ten young men. David said to the young men, “Go up to Carmel, go to Nabal, and greet him in my name.”
Say this to him: ‘To one who lives [?]. Peace to you and your household.
“Your shepherds were with us, and we did not harm them. Nothing of theirs went missing during all the days they were in the wilderness.”
“Ask your servants, and they will tell you. Now let the young men find favor in your eyes, because we have come on a festive day. Give whatever you wish to your servants and to your son David.”
David’s young men came and spoke all these words to Nabal in David’s name.
Nabal answered David's servants, “Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse? These days there are many servants rebelling against their masters.”
“Should I take my bread, my water, and the meat I slaughtered for my shearers, and give them to men whose origins I do not know?”
David’s young men went back on their way and told David all these things.

David said to the men with him, “Each of you, strap on your sword!” They strapped on their swords, and David also strapped on his sword. About four hundred men went up after David, while two hundred stayed with the supplies.
One of the young servants told Abigail, Nabal's wife, “David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, but he treated them with contempt.”
“The men were very good to us. They did not harm us or cause us to lose anything during all the days we traveled with them while we were in the wilderness.”
“They were a wall around us, both night and day, during all the days we were with them tending the sheep.”
“Now consider and see what you should do, because disaster has been brought upon our master and his entire household.” Nabal was with the shepherds.

Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two wineskins of wine, five prepared sheep, five seahs of roasted grain, a hundred cheeses, and two hundred fig cakes, and loaded them onto a donkey.
She said to the young men, “Go ahead of me. I am coming behind you.” But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
She was riding the donkey and coming down a sheltered part of the mountain, while David and his men were coming up toward her, and she met them.
David had said, “It was in vain that we guarded everything he had in the wilderness, so that nothing of all he had went missing. He has repaid us with evil for good.”
“May the LORD do this to his servant David, and more besides, if by morning anyone belonging to him who urinates against a wall is left alive.”
When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got down from the donkey. She fell facedown before David and bowed to the ground.

She fell at his feet and said, “I beg you, my lord, let the blame be on me, my lord. Let your servant speak before you about this man Nabal, for he is just like his name. His name is Nabal, and disgraceful behavior goes with him. But I, your servant, did not see the young men whom my lord sent.”

“Now, my lord, as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, my lord, the LORD has delivered you so that you will not become involved in bloodshed. Now, my lord, may your enemies and those who seek to harm you become like Nabal.”
Now, this gift your servant has brought to my lord—give this gift to the young men who follow my lord.
“Forgive your servant's offense, for the LORD will surely establish a lasting house for my lord, because my lord fights the LORD's battles. No evil has been found in you throughout your days.”

“A man has set out to pursue you and seek your life, but may my lord's life be bound in the bundle of the living with the LORD your God. May the LORD throw the lives of your enemies into the pocket of a sling.”
And when the LORD does good to you, my lord, and appoints you ruler over Israel,
“Let this not become a cause of distress or a stumbling block to your heart through shedding blood without cause. When the LORD does good to you, remember your servant.”
David said to Abigail, “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me.”
“Blessed be your good judgment, and blessed be you, who have kept me today from becoming involved in bloodshed and have freed my hands from blood today.”

“But as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has kept me from harming you, if you had not hurried and come to meet me, no one belonging to Nabal who urinates against a wall would have remained by morning light.”
David accepted from her hands what she had brought and said to her, “Go up to your house in peace. See, I have listened to you and granted your request.”
Abigail came to Nabal, and there he was holding a feast in his house like a king's feast. Nabal was in good spirits and very drunk, so she told him nothing until dawn.
When morning came and the wine had worn off, his wife told him these things. His heart died within him, and he became like a stone.
About ten days passed, and the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.

David heard that Nabal had died and said, “Blessed be the LORD, who has upheld my case against the insult I received from Nabal and has kept his servant from doing evil. The LORD has brought Nabal’s wickedness back on his own head.” Then David sent word to Abigail, asking to take her as his wife.
David’s servants came to Abigail at Carmel and said to her, “David has sent us to you to take you as his wife.”
She rose, bowed with her face to the ground, and said, “Here is your servant, ready to be a maidservant and wash the feet of my lord’s servants.”
Abigail quickly got up and mounted a donkey, with five of her young women following her on foot. She went with David’s messengers and became his wife.
David also married Ahinoam from Jezreel, and both women became his wives.
Saul had given his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.
The Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and said to him, “Look, David is hiding on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon.”
Saul rose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph, taking three thousand chosen men of Israel with him to search for David in the wilderness of Ziph.
Saul camped on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon, beside the road. David was staying in the wilderness, and he saw that Saul had come after him into the wilderness.
David sent out spies and learned that Saul had come after him.

David rose and came to the place where Saul had camped. David saw the place where Saul and Abner son of Ner, Saul’s army commander, were sleeping. Saul was sleeping on the track, with the troops camped around him.
David said to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, “Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?” Abishai said, “I will go down with you.”
David and Abishai came to the troops at night. There was Saul, sleeping on the track, with his spear set in the ground beside his head. Abner and the troops were sleeping around him.
Abishai said to David, “Today your God has handed your enemy over to you. Now let me strike him once with this spear that is in the ground. I will not need to strike him a second time.”
David said to Abishai, “Do not kill him, because no one can raise his hand against the Lord’s anointed and remain innocent.”
David said, “As the LORD lives, the LORD himself will strike him, or his day will come and he will die, or he will be struck in battle and die.”
“The LORD forbid that I should raise my hand against the LORD’s anointed! Now take the spear beside his head and the water jar, and let us go.”
David took the spear and the jar from beside Saul’s head, and they went away. No one saw them or knew about it or woke up, because they were all sleeping: a sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them.
David went away from Saul and stood on the top of the mountain, a great distance away.
David called out to the king and to Abner son of Ner, saying, “Will you not answer, Abner?” Abner answered, “Who are you, calling out to the king?”
David said to Abner, “Look, you are a mighty warrior! Who is like you in all Israel? Why did you not guard your lord the king? Someone came today to kill the king, your lord.”

“You have not done well. As the LORD lives, you deserve to die, because you did not guard your lord, the LORD’s anointed. Now look: where are the king’s spear and the water jar that were beside his head?”
Saul heard David’s voice and said to him, “Is that your voice, my son David?” He said, “It is my voice, my lord the king.”
David said, “Why are you pursuing your servant, my lord? What have I done? What evil have I committed?

“Now let my lord the king listen to his servant’s words. If the LORD has stirred you up against me, let us present an offering. But if human beings have done so, may they be cursed before the LORD, because they have driven me away so that I cannot share in the LORD’s inheritance, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’”
“Now do not let my blood fall to the ground away from the LORD’s presence. For the king of Israel has come out to search for a single flea, as someone hunts a partridge in the mountains.”

Saul said to David, “I have sinned. Come back, my son David, for I will not harm you again, because my life was precious in your eyes today. Look, I have acted foolishly and have sinned very greatly.”
David answered, “Here is the king’s spear. Let one of the young men come over and take it.
“May the LORD repay each man for his righteousness and faithfulness. The LORD handed you over to me today, but I was unwilling to raise my hand against the LORD’s anointed.”
Just as your life was highly valued in my eyes today, so may my life be highly valued in the Lord’s eyes.”
Saul said to David, “Blessed are you, my son! You have indeed acted, and you have indeed prevailed.” David went on his way, and Saul returned home.

David said to himself, “Now I may one day fall into Saul’s hands. There is nothing better for me than to escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will grow tired of searching for me throughout the territory of Israel, and I will escape from his hands.”
David set out and crossed over, with the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath.
David lived with Achish in Gath, along with his men, the members of David’s household, and his two wives: Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail, Nabal’s wife, from Carmel.
Saul was told that David had gone down to Gath, and he stopped searching for him.

David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your eyes, let me be given a place in one of the towns in the wilderness, and I will live there. Your servant should not live with you in the royal city."
That day Achish gave him Ziklag. For this reason Ziklag has belonged to the king of Judah to this day.
The length of time David lived in the land of the Philistines was a year and four months.
David and his men went up and raided Geshur, Gedol, and Amalek, for these had been the inhabitants of the land from ancient times. They raided Geshur and as far as the land of Egypt.
David devastated the land and left neither man nor woman alive. He took sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing. Then David returned and came to Achish.
Achish said to David, "Where have you been today?" David said, "Against the Negev of Judah, the Negev of Jerahmeel, and the Negev of Keilah."

David left neither man nor woman alive to come to Gath, saying, "Otherwise they may report on us and say, 'This is what David did.'" This was his practice throughout the time David lived in the land of the Philistines.
Achish trusted David and said, “He has certainly made himself hateful to his people Israel. Now he will be my servant forever.”

In those days the Philistines gathered their armies for battle in the valley, to fight against Israel. Achish said to David, "You must understand that you and your men will go out with me into the army."
David said to Achish, "Then you will know what your servant will do." Achish said to David, "Then I will make you my personal bodyguard for life."
Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in his tomb in Ramah. Saul had removed the mediums and diviners from the land.
The Philistines gathered, came, and camped at Shechem. Saul gathered all Israel, and they camped at Gilgal.
Saul saw the Philistine armies and was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
He inquired of the LORD, but he did not answer him, whether by dreams, by fire, or by prophets.
Saul said to his servants, "Find me a woman who brings up spirits, so that I can go to her and consult her." His servants said to him, "There is a woman who brings up spirits at Endor."

Saul took off his clothes and put on other clothes. He went with two men, and they came to the woman at night. Saul said to her, "Tell my fortune through a spirit, and bring up for me the person I name to you."
The woman said to him, "You know what Saul has done, how he has removed the mediums and diviners from the land. Why are you setting a trap for my life, to have me put to death?"
Saul swore to her by the Lord, saying, “As the Lord lives, no punishment will come upon you for this matter.”
The woman said, “Whom shall I bring up for you?” He said, “Bring Samuel up for me.”
The woman saw Samuel and cried out loudly. She said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!"
The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What have you seen?" The woman said to Saul, "I have seen gods coming up from the earth."
He said to her, "What does he look like?" She said to him, "An old man is coming up, wrapped in a cloak." Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he fell facedown on the ground and bowed.

Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" Saul said, "I am in great distress. The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has withdrawn from me and no longer answers me, either through prophets or in a dream. I sought you and called you so that you would tell me what to do."
Samuel said to Saul, “Why are you asking me, when the LORD has departed from you and is with your fellow?”
The LORD has done as he said through me. He has torn the kingdom from your hand and given it to your fellow, David.
Because you did not obey the LORD and did not carry out his fierce anger against Amalek, the LORD has done this to you today.
The LORD will also hand Israel over with you to the Philistines. Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The LORD will also hand the army of Israel over to the Philistines.

Saul was overcome with alarm and fell facedown on the ground. He was terribly afraid because of Samuel's words. He also had no strength left, because he had eaten no food all that day and all that night.
The woman came to Saul and saw that he was terribly afraid. She said to him, "Your servant has obeyed you. I have put my life in your hands and listened to the words you spoke to me.
Now you too must listen to your servant. Let me set a piece of bread before you. Eat, so that you will have strength as you go on your journey."
He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his servants, together with the woman, urged him, and he listened to them. He rose from the ground and sat on the bed.
The woman had a fattened calf in her house. She hurried and slaughtered it, then took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread.
She served it to Saul and his servants. They ate, got up, and went away that night.
The Philistines gathered all their armies at Aphek, while Israel was camped by the spring in Jezreel.
The rulers of the Philistines were marching past with their hundreds and thousands, and David and his men were marching at the rear with Achish.

The commanders of the Philistines said to Achish, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish said to the commanders of the Philistines, "This is David, the servant of Saul king of Israel, who has been with us for some time now, for months. I have found no fault in him from the day he came to me until today."

The Philistine commanders were angry with him and said to him, “Send the man away. Let him return to the place where you stationed him. He must not go into battle with us, or he may become our enemy in battle. For how could this man regain his master’s favor except with our own heads?”
“Is this not David, about whom the women of Israel sang with tambourines, saying, ‘Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”

Achish called David and said to him, “As the LORD lives, you are upright, and I am pleased with your going out and coming in with me in battle. I have found no evil in you from the day you came to us until today. But the rulers do not approve of you.”
Now turn back and go in peace. Do nothing that displeases the Philistine rulers.”
David said to Achish, “What have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I came before you until today, that I should not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?”
Achish answered David, “I know that you are as good in my eyes as an angel of God. Nevertheless, the Philistine commanders say, ‘He must not go into battle with us.’”
“Now rise early in the morning, along with your master’s servants who came with you on the journey. When it is light for you, leave.”
David and his men rose early to leave for the land of the Philistines, while the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
When David and his men came to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had raided the Negev and Ziklag and burned them with fire.
They took captive the people in them, from the youngest to the oldest, and killed the men. They led the captives away and went on their way.
David and his men came to the town and found it burned with fire, and their wives, sons, and daughters had been taken captive.
David and the people raised their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep.
David’s two wives had also been taken captive: Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
David was deeply distressed because the people spoke of stoning him, for all the people were heartsick over their sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God.
He said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Bring me the ephod.” Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
David inquired of the LORD, saying, “Should I pursue this raiding party? Will I overtake it?” He said to him, “Pursue it, for you will soon overtake it and rescue the captives.”
David went with the six hundred men who were with him. They came to the Besor stream, and David left two hundred men there.
David continued the pursuit with four hundred men, while the two hundred men who remained stayed behind and waited, without crossing the Besor stream.
They found an Egyptian man in a field and brought him to David. They gave him bread, and he ate. They also gave him water to drink and two cheeses.
He ate, and his strength returned, for he had eaten no bread and drunk no water for three days and three nights.
David said to him, “Whose servant are you, and where have you come from?” He said, “I am an Egyptian young man, a slave of an Amalekite. My master abandoned me because I fell sick three days ago.”
Look, we have come from the Negev of Judah, from the Negev of Caleb, and from Ziklag, which we burned with fire.

David said to him, “Will you lead me down to this raiding party?” He said to him, “Swear to me by the LORD that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master, and I will show you this raiding party.”

David swore to him, and he led him down. There they were, spread out over the land, eating, drinking, and celebrating all the great plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah.
David attacked them from behind, from morning until evening. None of them escaped except four hundred men who mounted camels and fled.
David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives.
Nothing of theirs was missing; David brought everything back.
David drove all the sheep and cattle ahead of that livestock, and they said, “This is David’s plunder.”

David came to the two hundred men who had remained to guard the equipment, whom he had stationed on the road to Besor to keep watch. They came out to meet David and the people with him. David and the people approached and greeted them.

The wicked and lawless men among those who had gone with David spoke up and said, “Because they did not go with us, they must not be given a share of the plunder we recovered. Let each man take only his wife and children.”
David said, “Do not do this, brothers, with what the LORD has given us. He protected us and handed over to us the raiding party that came against us.”
“Who would listen to this proposal of yours? The share of the one who goes down into battle is to be the same as the share of the one who stays beside the equipment. They will share alike.”
From that day onward, David established this as a statute and a rule, which remains to this day.
David came to Ziklag and sent some of the plunder to the elders of Judah and their friends, saying, “Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies.”
He sent it to those in Bethel, those in Beth-ramoth of the Negev, and those in Beth-ai;
And to those in Aroer, and to those in Siphmoth, and to those in Eshtemoa.
to those in Rachal, those in the towns of the Jerahmeelites, and those in the towns of the Kenites;
to those in Hormah, those in Rab-ashan, and those in Taanach;
to those in Hebron, and to all the places where David and his men had traveled.
The Philistines were fighting against Israel. The men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines killed Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua, Saul’s sons.
The battle grew fierce around Saul. The archers with their bows overtook him, and he was very afraid of the archers.

Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and stab me with it, so that these uncircumcised men do not come and kill me and mock me.” But his armor-bearer would not, because he was very afraid. So Saul took his sword and fell on it.
When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his sword and died.
So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his servants died together that day.

When the Israelites on the other side of the Jordan valley saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their towns and fled. The Philistines came and settled in them.
The next day the Philistines came to strip the dead and found Saul and his three sons lying on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head and stripped off his armor. They sent word throughout the land of the Philistines to announce the good news among the people and in the temple of their idols.
They put his armor in the temple of the goddesses and fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.
The inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul and his sons.
All the warriors set out and traveled all night. They took Saul’s body and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, brought them to Jabesh, and burned them there.
They took their bones and buried them beneath the almond tree in Jabesh, and they fasted for seven days.
